title: THEY THREW JOSEPH INTO A PIT… BUT THEY COULDN’T BURY GOD’S PLAN: Why His Story Contains So Many Parallels Christians Associate With Jesus
paragraphs:
THEY THREW JOSEPH INTO A PIT… BUT THEY COULDN’T BURY GOD’S PLAN: Why His Story Contains So Many Parallels Christians Associate With Jesus
Long before a cross stood outside Jerusalem, Genesis told the haunting story of a beloved son rejected by his own, sold for silver, falsely accused, brought low, exalted to power, and ultimately used to save the very people who wounded him. Joseph was not Jesus. But once you have seen the pattern, it becomes very difficult to read his story the same way again.
Imagine hearing your own brothers discussing what to do with you.
Not strangers.
Not enemies.
Your brothers.
The people who know your childhood. The people who ate at the same table. The people whose blood runs through the same family line.
And they hate you enough to make you disappear.
Joseph is seventeen when the story takes its terrible turn.
Genesis tells us:
וְיִשְׂרָאֵל אָהַב אֶת־יוֹסֵף מִכָּל־בָּנָיו
Ve-Yisra’el ahav et-Yosef mikol-banav…

“Israel loved Joseph more than all his sons…”
—Genesis 37:3
The Hebrew verb אָהַב (’ahav) means “loved.”
Joseph is the deeply loved son of his father.
And that love becomes part of the scandal.
His brothers see it.
They resent it.
Then Joseph tells them about dreams in which God appears to be pointing toward his future exaltation.
Their resentment hardens.
Genesis 37:11 says:
וַיְקַנְאוּ־בוֹ אֶחָיו
Vayqanne’u-vo echav.
“His brothers were jealous of him.”
Jealousy.
That detail matters more than we sometimes realize.

Because centuries later, when Stephen stands before Israel’s leaders in Acts 7, he deliberately reaches backward into Israel’s history and reminds them that the patriarchs became jealous of Joseph and sold him into Egypt.
But God was with Joseph.
Stephen is speaking while confronting another tragedy of rejection—the rejection of Jesus Christ.
The point is not that Joseph secretly was Jesus.
He wasn’t.
Joseph was a sinful human being who needed God’s grace just like every other descendant of Adam.
Jesus is the sinless Son of God, the eternal Word who became flesh, the promised Messiah, crucified for our sins and raised from the dead.
Joseph cannot save your soul.
Jesus can.
But Joseph’s life forms an extraordinary biblical pattern that Christians have long recognized as resembling the greater story that reaches its fulfillment in Christ.
And maybe that is why Joseph’s story hurts so deeply.
Because before it reminds us of Jesus…
it reminds many of us of ourselves.
You know what betrayal feels like.
Maybe nobody threw you into a literal pit.
But somebody you trusted abandoned you when you needed them.
Somebody talked about you behind your back.
Somebody took what you told them privately and turned it into ammunition.
Maybe family members treated you like an outsider.
Maybe you were falsely accused.
Maybe someone destroyed your reputation and then slept peacefully while you spent nights wondering how you would ever recover.
Maybe you have stared at the ceiling and asked:
“God, if You love me, why did You allow this?”
Joseph understands the question.
His brothers see him approaching in Genesis 37 and say:
הִנֵּה בַּעַל הַחֲלֹמוֹת הַלָּזֶה בָּא
Hinneh ba‘al haḥalomot hallazeh ba.
“Look, this dreamer is coming.”
Then comes the murderous suggestion:
“Come now, let us kill him…”
Think about that.
The one who would eventually become the instrument God used to preserve their lives was the one they wanted dead.
The future deliverer of the family was rejected by the family.
And here the Christian ear begins hearing an echo.
Jesus came to His own, and His own did not receive Him.
The One through whom salvation would come was rejected by the people He came to save.
Joseph’s brothers wanted his dreams silenced.
Jesus’ enemies wanted His claims silenced.
Joseph was stripped of the special garment associated with his father’s favor.
Jesus was stripped before His crucifixion.
Joseph was handed over by people who should have loved him.
Jesus was handed over to His enemies.
Joseph was sold.
Jesus was betrayed for money.
But accuracy matters here.
Sometimes Christians say, “Joseph was sold for thirty pieces of silver just like Jesus.”
That is not what Genesis says.
Genesis 37:28 records Joseph’s sale for twenty pieces of silver.
Judas later agrees to betray Jesus for thirty pieces of silver in Matthew 26:15.
The parallel is therefore not an identical price.
It is betrayal associated with silver.
That distinction matters because we do not need to exaggerate Scripture to make Scripture powerful.
Truth is already powerful enough.
Then Joseph disappears into Egypt.
From the brothers’ perspective, the story is finished.
They have removed him.
His dreams appear buried.
His future appears stolen.
His father believes him dead.
But there is a sentence running quietly through Joseph’s suffering that changes everything:
וַיְהִי יְהוָה אֶת־יוֹסֵף
Vayehi YHWH et-Yosef.
“The LORD was with Joseph.”
—Genesis 39:2
Read that again.
God did not prevent Joseph from being sold.
God was with him while he was sold.
God did not prevent him from entering Egypt.
God was with him in Egypt.
God did not immediately remove every injustice.
God remained with him through the injustice.
Somebody reading this needs that distinction.
You may have mistaken the presence of suffering for the absence of God.
Joseph’s story refuses that conclusion.
The pit was real.
The slavery was real.
The betrayal was real.
And God was still there.
Then Joseph faces another test.
Potiphar’s wife attempts to seduce him.
Joseph refuses.
His reason is deeply theological:
“How then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?”
Joseph understands something our generation desperately needs to recover.
Sin is not merely breaking a religious rule.
Sin is ultimately against God.
And Joseph would rather lose his position than betray his God.
So he runs.
And somehow…
doing the right thing makes his circumstances worse.
She falsely accuses him.
Joseph goes to prison.
That is one of the most painful realities in Scripture because it destroys a shallow version of Christianity that says obedience always produces immediate comfort.
Sometimes you obey God and lose something.
Sometimes integrity costs you.
Sometimes refusing temptation does not earn applause.
Sometimes holiness gets misunderstood.
Sometimes you do the right thing and still end up crying.
Joseph resisted sexual sin and landed in prison.
Jesus lived in perfect righteousness and was condemned.
Again, Joseph is not equal to Christ.
Joseph’s righteousness is creaturely and dependent upon God.
Christ’s sinlessness is perfect.
Yet the pattern of the righteous sufferer becomes increasingly difficult to ignore.
Joseph suffers under false accusation.
Jesus suffers under false testimony and unjust condemnation.
Joseph descends.
Then descends further.
Favorite son.
Slave.
Prisoner.
You can almost feel his life moving downward.
Until suddenly God reverses everything.
Pharaoh dreams.
Nobody can solve the mystery.
Joseph is remembered.
The prisoner is summoned.
The forgotten man stands before the most powerful ruler in Egypt.
And Joseph does something beautiful.
He refuses to steal God’s glory.
When Pharaoh suggests that Joseph can interpret dreams, Joseph essentially answers:
It is not in me.
God will give Pharaoh the answer.
The man who has every human reason to become bitter has not abandoned his God.
The man betrayed by family still trusts God.
The man falsely accused still honors God.
The man forgotten in prison still gives God the glory.
Then comes the reversal.
Joseph interprets Pharaoh’s dreams.
Seven years of abundance are coming.
Then seven years of devastating famine.
Egypt must prepare.
Pharaoh recognizes the wisdom God has given Joseph and raises the prisoner to astonishing authority.
The rejected brother becomes ruler.
The humiliated one is exalted.
The one pushed downward is raised upward.
And again…
Christians hear an echo.
Jesus was rejected.
Jesus was humiliated.
Jesus was crucified.
Jesus truly died and was buried.
But death did not have the final word.
God raised Him from the dead.
Philippians 2 describes Christ humbling Himself to the point of death—even death on a cross—and then declares that God highly exalted Him.
Joseph moves from humiliation toward exaltation.
Jesus moves through the ultimate humiliation of the cross into resurrection glory and exaltation.
But Jesus is infinitely greater.
Joseph emerges from prison to administer grain.
Jesus emerges victorious over death itself.
Joseph receives authority from Pharaoh.
Jesus declares that all authority in heaven and on earth has been given to Him.
Joseph helps preserve physical life during famine.
Jesus gives eternal life to those who come to Him in faith.
And then the story becomes almost unbearably emotional.
The famine arrives.
People become desperate.
Eventually Joseph’s brothers come to Egypt looking for food.
They do not recognize him.
Think about the irony.
They are standing before the brother they rejected.
Their survival now depends upon the one they betrayed.
The man they discarded has become the man holding the grain they desperately need.
The rejected one has become the source through whom their preservation will come.
And Joseph recognizes them.
He could destroy them.
He could expose them.
He could humiliate them publicly.
He could say:
“Now you know how it feels.”
Anyone who has ever been deeply wounded understands the temptation.
There is something inside fallen humanity that wants the person who hurt us to experience the pain they caused.
We call it justice.
Sometimes it is really revenge wearing respectable clothing.
Joseph tests his brothers, and the narrative shows that God has been working on them too.
The men who once sold a brother begin showing signs of changed hearts.
Judah—the very brother who proposed selling Joseph—eventually offers himself in place of Benjamin.
And Joseph can no longer contain himself.
Genesis 45 says he weeps.
Not politely.
Not quietly.
He weeps so loudly that the Egyptians hear him.
Then he says the words his brothers never expected:
אֲנִי יוֹסֵף
Ani Yosef.
“I am Joseph.”
Can you imagine that room?
Their blood must have gone cold.
The brother they betrayed is alive.
Not merely alive.
Powerful.
And they are standing helplessly before him.
This should be judgment.
This should be revenge.
This should be the moment Joseph destroys them.
Instead…
grace enters the room.
“Come near to me, please.”
Joseph tells them not to be distressed or angry with themselves for selling him there, because God had sent him ahead for the preservation of life.
Joseph does not pretend their evil was good.
That distinction is essential.
The brothers sinned.
They betrayed him.
They lied.
They caused extraordinary suffering.
Joseph does not rename evil.
He recognizes something greater:
human evil had not defeated divine providence.
Years later he summarizes the mystery in one of Genesis’ most unforgettable declarations.
Genesis 50:20:
וְאַתֶּם חֲשַׁבְתֶּם עָלַי רָעָה אֱלֹהִים חֲשָׁבָהּ לְטֹבָה
Ve’attem ḥashavtem ‘alai ra‘ah; Elohim ḥashavah letovah.
“You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good.”
Notice what Joseph does not say.
He does not say:
“It wasn’t evil.”
He says it was evil.
But evil did not get the final sentence.
God did.
That is where Joseph’s story begins blazing with Gospel-shaped significance.
Because what is the cross?
Human beings committed horrifying evil against the sinless Son of God.
Judas betrayed Him.
Leaders plotted against Him.
False testimony was used.
Pilate surrendered Him to crucifixion.
Soldiers mocked Him.
Human beings drove nails through Him.
None of that evil became morally good simply because God accomplished salvation through it.
And yet Acts 2:23 says Jesus was delivered up according to God’s definite plan and foreknowledge while holding His killers morally responsible.
Human wickedness and divine sovereignty meet at Calvary without God becoming the author of evil.
Men meant evil.
God accomplished redemption.
The cross looked like history’s greatest defeat.
It became the place where Christ bore our sins.
The grave looked like the end.
Then Sunday came.
This is why Joseph’s story reaches beyond an inspirational message about surviving difficult seasons.
Joseph is not merely telling you:
“Hang on. Your promotion is coming.”
That interpretation can become dangerously shallow.
Not every Christian will become wealthy.
Not every false accusation will be publicly corrected in this life.
Not every believer who suffers will receive Joseph’s earthly reversal.
Some faithful Christians have died poor, persecuted, imprisoned, forgotten by history.
Christian hope is greater than earthly promotion.
Joseph’s story ultimately trains our eyes to look for the God who can bring His redemptive purposes through circumstances human beings intended for destruction.
And Jesus is the supreme revelation of that truth.
Joseph forgave brothers who deserved judgment.
At the cross, Jesus prayed for those crucifying Him.
Joseph provided bread to hungry people.
Jesus calls Himself the Bread of Life.
Joseph’s brothers came desperate for food they could not provide for themselves.
We come to Christ spiritually bankrupt, unable to purchase forgiveness with morality, religion, good intentions, church attendance, charity, tears, promises, or religious performance.
Joseph’s brothers discovered that the brother they rejected was the one through whom God would preserve them.
The Gospel announces something infinitely greater:
the Christ humanity rejected is the only Savior humanity has.
There is no salvation in Joseph.
There is salvation in Jesus Christ.
And perhaps the most frightening similarity is not between Joseph and Jesus.
Perhaps it is between Joseph’s brothers…
and us.
They were guilty.
So are we.
They had sinned against the beloved son.
So have we sinned against God.
They could not undo their past.
Neither can you.
You cannot crawl backward through time and unsay the words.
You cannot unwatch what you watched.
You cannot undo the affair.
You cannot remove every scar you caused.
You cannot become sexually pure retroactively.
You cannot unlie.
You cannot unbetray.
You cannot erase the years you ignored God.
You cannot save yourself by promising that tomorrow’s version of you will compensate for yesterday’s rebellion.
This is why Christianity is not fundamentally a message of self-improvement.
It is news of rescue.
The Gospel does not say:
“Fix yourself until God can tolerate you.”
It says that while we were sinners, Christ died for us.
Jesus bore sin.
Jesus died.
Jesus was buried.
Jesus rose.
And forgiveness is offered through Him to repentant sinners who trust in Him.
Maybe you have spent years hiding from God because you believe He is waiting to humiliate you.
Look again at Joseph saying to his terrified brothers:
“Come near.”
Then look beyond Joseph.
Look at Jesus.
The wounds in Christ’s hands are not evidence that your sin was insignificant.
They are evidence that grace was unimaginably costly.
God does not forgive because sin does not matter.
At Calvary we discover just how much it matters.
And there we discover how astonishing His mercy is.
This is From Scandal to Grace.
Not because God calls scandal righteousness.
Not because consequences magically disappear.
Not because repentance is optional.
But because Jesus Christ takes guilty people who deserve judgment, cleanses those who come to Him, forgives sinners, gives them a new identity, and begins transforming their lives by His grace.
Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the old pages never happened.
By refusing to let those pages determine the ending.
Maybe your story contains betrayal.
Jesus still rewrites.
Maybe your story contains sexual sin.
Jesus still rewrites.
Maybe addiction has embarrassed you.
Jesus still rewrites.
Maybe you destroyed trust.
Jesus still rewrites.
Maybe church people hurt you and you responded by running from God.
Jesus still rewrites.
Maybe you smile online while privately wondering whether God could possibly want you anymore.
Jesus still rewrites.
Repentance does not mean pretending.
It means coming into the light.
Grace does not mean permission to continue comfortably in sin.
Grace teaches us to leave sin and follow Christ.
Forgiveness is not God shrugging at rebellion.
Forgiveness was purchased at the cross.
And resurrection means your worst chapter does not have authority to declare the final sentence over a life surrendered to Jesus Christ.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to explain your entire story publicly.
But you can stop pretending.
Your testimony may become the sentence another wounded person desperately needs to read tonight.
Do not keep this article trapped on this page.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It does not.
It cannot.
But if you genuinely want to glorify God with what He has placed in your hands, one practical response is to help biblical truth travel farther.
Somebody is carrying shame.
Somebody believes their scandal has become their identity.
Somebody is close to giving up.
Send it privately to the friend who would never comment publicly.
It does not make God love you more.
It does not make you more saved.
Jesus alone saves.
But supporting Gospel-centered work can be one practical way of helping more Scripture-centered resources reach people who desperately need Christ.
Come to Jesus.
Not merely to Christian content.
Not merely to Gospel Warrior.
Not merely to inspirational stories.
Come to Christ.
Joseph’s story is beautiful precisely because Joseph is not the destination.
The road keeps going.
Past the pit.
Past Egypt.
Past the famine.
Past Genesis.
Through prophets and promises.
Until eventually another beloved Son appears.
Rejected.
Betrayed.
Condemned.
Humiliated.
And crucified.
Then the stone is rolled away.
The tomb is empty.
Jesus Christ is risen.
Joseph could tell his frightened brothers:
“I am Joseph.”
The risen Christ announces something infinitely greater:
He is alive forevermore.
And because He lives, repentance is not the funeral of your future.
It can become the doorway into a completely different life.
So perhaps the sentence you need to remember is not:
“They hurt me.”
Not:
“I failed.”
Not:
“I ruined everything.”
Not:
“My family rejected me.”
Not:
“My past disqualifies me.”

Remember instead the God revealed throughout Scripture—the God whose sovereignty is not defeated by pits, prisons, betrayal, false accusations, crosses, graves, or the wicked intentions of human beings.
What others meant for evil does not become good simply because God touched your story.
But evil does not get sovereignty.
God does.
And at the center of His redemptive plan stands Jesus Christ.
So repent.
Come home.
Forgive where Christ calls you to forgive.
Confess what needs confessing.
Leave what needs leaving.
Repair what can be repaired.
Stop hiding.
Receive the grace you cannot earn.
And follow Jesus.
And comment before you leave.
Not for an algorithm alone.
For the person reading beneath you.
Tell them:
“God is not finished with me.”
Because maybe someone needs to see another wounded Christian refuse to surrender.
Maybe someone needs proof that repentance is still possible.
Maybe someone needs to know that grace still enters ugly stories.
Maybe someone needs to discover what Joseph learned before us…
and what the empty tomb declares beyond Joseph:
The pit can become part of the testimony, but it never gets to write the ending when the Author of redemption is still holding the pen.
